title: The Payatas Foot Rugs That Became Rags2Riches in 2007
dek: A group of young founders in Manila saw women weaving rugs from scrap for a few pesos a day and started a company with them on 10,000 pesos.

story.event: Starting a business with Payatas rug weavers to cut out middlemen and turn scrap rugs into designed products
story.summary: In 2007 Reese Fernandez (later Fernandez-Ruiz) and eight co-founders started Rags2Riches with 10,000 pesos after meeting women in Payatas, Quezon City, who wove foot rugs from scrap fabric but, dependent on middlemen, earned only about 10 to 16 pesos a day. Working with the weavers, they improved the rugs, sold them at a bazaar, and with the designer Rajo Laurel turned the woven scraps into bags and accessories, paying artisans for their labour whether or not pieces sold.
paragraphs: In Payatas, a community in Quezon City that lives alongside a landfill, women were weaving foot rugs from scraps of fabric. Many were mothers who wanted work they could do at home. Reese Fernandez (later Fernandez-Ruiz), a management student and scholar at the Ateneo de Manila University, met some of them on a university-organised trip to look at livelihood projects there.

What she and her friends found was a sum that did not add up. Middlemen controlled both the scrap cloth and the market, so the weavers paid too much for materials and took whatever price was offered. By her later account, a woman might weave ten rugs in a day and earn 12 to 16 pesos for all of it. "R2R started because of an irritation and a social problem," she said. Looking back, she described the choice as doing nothing because the problem was so big, or doing something, even if it was small.

In 2007 nine co-founders, among them a Jesuit priest, people working for multinationals and Mark Ruiz, whom she later married, started Rags2Riches with 10,000 pesos. Fernandez, the youngest and a fresh graduate, began as a part-time volunteer, then decided to give her working life to it so that it would not be cut off halfway as a nice project. The hardest part, she has said, was trust: the women had been promised much before and let down, so the founders went, listened and exchanged ideas.

The first change came from a long brainstorm with the weavers: plain-coloured rugs of better quality. At a bazaar, sold with their story, 700 pieces went in two hours, she recalled. Then the designer Rajo Laurel began turning the woven scraps into bags, vanity kits and wine holders. "When he looked at the rags, he saw something that none of us had ever seen," she said. The company paid artisans for their labour whether or not the pieces sold, and in 2010 The Philippine Star reported that they could earn five times what rugs and rags had brought them.

quote.text: When we define a man by the market value of the service we can expect of him, we know him imperfectly. With this limited knowledge of him it becomes easy for us to be unjust to him
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore warns that knowing people only by what their work is worth on the market makes injustice easy. The middlemen's prices in Payatas were that narrow knowledge in practice; Rags2Riches began by sitting with the weavers long enough to know them as more than a price per rug.

reflection: The founders did not begin with a fashion label. They began with a day's weaving paid in a handful of pesos, and with the slow work of being trusted by women who had been let down before. The bazaar, the designer and the steadier pay all came after the listening.

There is usually someone whose work holds yours up and whom it is easy to know only by what they cost. It may be worth asking what you actually know about that person beyond the service they provide, and whether they would say you had listened to them.
invitation: Ask one person whose work quietly supports yours what the hardest part of their job is this week. Listen to the whole answer before you say anything about fixing it.

cross_checks.claim: Rags2Riches was founded in Payatas in 2007
The weavers depended on middlemen and earned roughly 10 to 16 pesos a day
Building the artisans' trust was the founders' hardest early challenge
The designer Rajo Laurel helped turn the rags into bags and accessories

research_notes: Earnings before Rags2Riches differ slightly by source: Fernandez-Ruiz told Tatler (2022) that ten rugs a day brought 12 to 16 pesos; The Philippine Star (2020) gives 10 to 16 pesos a day; an artisan quoted in The Philippine Star (2013) recalled 10 to 12 pesos a day; Fernandez-Ruiz told the World Economic Forum (2018) about 20 US cents a day. These are consistent in scale; the story gives her Tatler figure and attributes it. Founding date: The Philippine Star (2010) says November 2007; MoneySense (2013) says started in 2007 and registered in January 2008; Tatler (2022) says 'about 14 years ago'. The story says 2007. Rajo Laurel: The Philippine Star (2013) says he offered his help, while the WEF Q&A says the founders took their idea to him; the story says only that he began designing the products. The '700 pieces in two hours' and the five-times earnings figure each come from one source and are attributed (her recollection; The Philippine Star, 2010). Later scale figures conflict (WEF 2018: more than 1,000 artisans trained; Tatler 2022: 200 artisans across eight communities), so the story uses neither. The company's own name is written Rags2Riches; she was Reese Fernandez at founding and later Fernandez-Ruiz. Funding is bootstrapped: 10,000 pesos and the founders' own money to incorporate, per MoneySense. The Inquirer and Devex profiles were not used because they return 403 to the verifier. Tagore wrote Sadhana in English; the passage is about knowing people only by their market value, applied here to the middlemen's prices.
